narrative:
The model estimates an 11% chance that you will fail your final year, which is low enough to trigger the requirement for remedial courses as a precaution. This prediction is driven primarily by three key aspects of your profile that the system weighs most heavily.

The strongest factor is that you have had no past class failures, which actually works in your favor by pulling the prediction toward passing. However, this positive influence is outweighed by two other elements. Your desire to pursue higher education also leans toward a better outcome, yet the model still sees risk because your weekly study time is less than two hours. This is substantially lower than the typical 2–5 hours that most students who ultimately pass tend to dedicate, and it is the main feature pushing the prediction toward failure.

In short, although your clean record of no previous failures and your ambition for further studies are recognized as strengths, the limited time you currently spend studying each week creates enough concern for the system to forecast a risk of not passing.

To improve, you should seriously consider increasing your weekly study hours, perhaps aiming for at least two to five hours as many successful students do. This single change could meaningfully strengthen your chances and potentially remove the need for remedial courses next year.
